content: 1. Glimepiride metabolism may vary among individuals, necessitating dose adjustments and close monitoring for hypoglycemia or worsening glycemic control, particularly in geriatric or renally impaired patients. 2. Elderly patients or those with renal impairment are at an increased risk of hypoglycemia when using glimepiride. Careful dose selection and titration, along with close monitoring, are essential in these populations. 3. There is limited information available regarding the compatibility of glimepiride with intravenous (IV) administrations. 4. An overdose of glimepiride, similar to other sulfonylureas, can result in severe hypoglycemia. Mild hypoglycemic episodes can be managed with oral glucose, while severe hypoglycemic reactions constitute medical emergencies requiring immediate treatment. 5. Severe hypoglycemia accompanied by coma, seizures, or neurological impairment should be treated with glucagon or intravenous glucose. Continued observation and additional carbohydrate intake may be necessary, as hypoglycemia can recur after apparent clinical recovery. 6. Glimepiride lowers blood glucose primarily by stimulating insulin release from pancreatic beta cells. 7. Glimepiride is an oral sulfonylurea containing the active ingredient glimepiride. Chemically, it is identified as 1-[(p-(2-(3-ethyl-4-methyl-2-oxo-3-pyrroline-1-carboxamido)ethyl)phenyl)sulfonyl]-3-(trans-4-methylcyclohexyl)urea with a molecular weight of 490.62. It is a white to yellowish-white, crystalline, odorless to practically odorless powder that is practically insoluble in water. 8. Glimepiride tablets contain inactive ingredients such as lactose monohydrate, sodium starch glycolate, povidone, and magnesium stearate. Additionally, 1 mg tablets contain ferric oxide red, 2 mg tablets contain ferric oxide yellow and FD&C Blue 2 aluminum lake, and 4 mg tablets contain FD&C Blue 2 aluminum lake. 9. In healthy individuals, the time to reach maximal effect (minimum blood glucose concentrations) is approximately 2 to 3 hours after a single oral dose of glimepiride. Clinical trials have assessed its effects on HbA1c, fasting plasma glucose, and postprandial glucose. 10. Pharmacokinetics studies show that peak drug concentrations (Cmax) occur 2 to 3 hours post-dose. When taken with meals, the mean Cmax and AUC (area under the curve) decrease by 8% and 9%, respectively. Glimepiride does not accumulate in serum with multiple dosing, and its pharmacokinetics are similar in healthy individuals and patients with type 2 diabetes. 11. Glimepiride clearance after oral administration remains consistent across the 1 mg to 8 mg dose range, indicating linear pharmacokinetics. In healthy individuals, intraand inter-individual variability in pharmacokinetic parameters ranges from 15% to 23% and 24% to 29%, respectively. 12. After intravenous dosing, the volume of distribution (Vd) is 8.8 L (113 mL/kg), and total body clearance (CL) is 47.8 mL/min. Protein binding exceeds 99.5%. 13. Glimepiride is completely metabolized via oxidative biotransformation. The major metabolites are the cyclohexyl hydroxy methyl derivative (M1) and the carboxyl derivative (M2). Cytochrome P450 2C9 is involved in the conversion of glimepiride to M1, which is further metabolized to M2 by cytosolic enzymes. M2 is inactive, while M1 retains about one-third of the pharmacological activity of glimepiride, though its clinical significance in humans is unclear. 14. After oral administration of radiolabeled glimepiride, approximately 60% of the total radioactivity is recovered in urine within 7 days, with M1 and M2 accounting for 80% to 90% of the radioactivity. The ratio of M1 to M2 in urine is approximately 3:2 or 4:1, depending on the individual. About 40% of the total radioactivity is recovered in feces, with M1 and M2 accounting for 70% of the radioactivity (M1 to M2 ratio of 1:3). No parent drug is recovered in urine or feces. 15. In patients, no significant biliary excretion of glimepiride or its M1 metabolite is observed after intravenous dosing. 16. In geriatric patients, pharmacokinetics of glimepiride do not differ significantly from younger patients. The mean AUC at steady state is approximately 13% lower in older patients, and weight-adjusted clearance is about 11% higher. 17. There are no differences in glimepiride pharmacokinetics between males and females when adjusted for body weight differences. 18. No studies have specifically assessed the effects of race on glimepiride pharmacokinetics. However, placebo-controlled trials show comparable reductions in HbA1c among Caucasians, Blacks, and Hispanics with type 2 diabetes. 19. In patients with renal impairment, glimepiride serum concentrations decrease with declining renal function. However, patients with severe renal impairment exhibit a 2.3-fold higher mean AUC for M1 and an 8.6-fold higher mean AUC for M2 compared to those with mild impairment. The half-lives of M1 and M2 increase as renal function decreases, while the terminal half-life of glimepiride remains unchanged. 20. In patients with hepatic impairment, the pharmacokinetics of glimepiride have not been adequately studied, and its effects remain unknown. 21. In obese patients, pharmacokinetics of glimepiride are similar to those in individuals with normal body weight in terms of Tmax, clearance, and volume of distribution. However, obese patients exhibit lower Cmax and AUC values compared to those with normal body weight.
